translations.text: Josiah celebrated the Passover for his God in Jerusalem and slaughtered the Passover offerings on the fourteenth day of the first month.
He stationed the priests in their vestments and arranged them according to their duties in the temple of the Lord.
He said to the Levites, “Serve the priests of Israel and sanctify them according to the arrangement of the Lord’s holy ark within the house that Solomon, son of King David, built.
You do not have to carry it on your shoulders. Now serve the Lord our God and bring joy to the people of Israel. Prepare yourselves according to your divisions and your families.

And according to the book of David king of Israel, in keeping with the greatness of his son Solomon, stand in his temple, you Levites, each in your own division, before your brothers, the Israelites, according to your appointed duties.”
Slaughter the Passover sacrifice and prepare the sacrifice for your brothers. Act according to the law of the Lord that was given to Moses.
Josiah gave the people who were there thirty thousand sheep and goats and three thousand cattle. Thus, by command, he gave these to the people, the priests, and the Levites from the king’s household.
Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Esielus, the leaders of the temple, gave the priests two thousand six hundred sheep and three hundred cattle for their Passover offerings.
Jeconiah, Shemaiah, his brother Nethanel, Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Joram, the leaders, gave the Levites one thousand sheep and seven hundred cattle for their Passover offerings.
In this way the priests and Levites did what was right according to his law, and the unleavened bread was distributed according to their tribes.
According to the leadership of their ancestral families, they brought offerings to the Lord before the people, as written in the book of Moses, and likewise in the morning.
They slaughtered the Passover offerings according to their law and cooked the sacrifices in pots and pans, with a pleasant aroma.
They distributed it to all the people, and afterward they prepared it for themselves and for their brothers, the priests, the descendants of Aaron.
The priests offered the fat sacrifices until late, and the Levites prepared portions for themselves and for their brothers, the priests descended from Aaron.
The priests responsible for singing, the descendants of Asaph, were at their appointed stations according to the arrangement of David, Asaph, Zechariah, and Eddinus, who were attached to the king.
The gatekeepers were at all the gates, and no one left his duties, because their brothers the Levites prepared portions for them.
They completed the sacrifice to the Lord.
On that day they brought their Passover offerings and also brought their sacrifices to the altar of the Lord, as King Josiah had commanded.
The Israelites who were present in those days celebrated their Passover and the Festival of Unleavened Bread for seven days.
No Passover like it had been celebrated in Israel since the time of Samuel the prophet.
None of the kings of Israel had celebrated a Passover like the one celebrated by Josiah, the priests, the Levites, the Jews, and all the Israelites who were there, who had moved to Jerusalem.
Josiah celebrated this Passover in the eighteenth year of his reign.
Josiah's work was carried out before his God with a heart full of fear of the Lord.

As written in earlier times concerning those who sinned and transgressed against the Lord more than all the nations and kingdoms, and provoked him to anger, the Lord established his word against Israel.
After all these deeds of Josiah, Pharaoh king of Egypt arose and undertook a campaign at Carchemish by the Euphrates River, and Josiah went out to meet them.
The king of Egypt sent word to him, saying, “What have I to do with you, king of Judah?
I was not sent against you by God the Lord, for I am fighting at the Euphrates River. Now God is with me, and God is here with me, and he will help me. Withdraw, and do not oppose God.”
Josiah refused to withdraw with his chariots and began to fight. He refused to listen to the words from the Lord’s mouth through Jeremiah the prophet.
But he stood to fight him in the wilderness with one other, and messengers came down to King Josiah.
The king said to his sons, “Take me out of the battle, for I am very weak.” His sons then took him out of the battle.
He was carried on his other chariot and entered Jerusalem. There he died and was buried in his father’s tomb.
They mourned Josiah throughout Judah, and Jeremiah wept for Josiah. They all lamented him, together with the women, down to this day. All the people of Israel were instructed to do this continually.

This was written in the prophetic accounts of the kings of Judah. Everything Josiah did—his deeds, his glory, his understanding of the law of the Lord, and what he did both earlier and later—was written in the book of the prophets of the kings of Israel and Judah.
The people took Jeconiah, Josiah’s son, and made him king in place of his father Josiah, when he was twenty-three years old.
He reigned over Israel in Jerusalem for three months. The king of Egypt entered Jerusalem with him to make him king.
He imposed on the people a tribute of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold.
The king of Egypt made his brother Jehoiakim king over Judah in Jerusalem.
Jehoiakim put the nobles in chains, seized his brother Zarion, and brought him from the land of Egypt.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king over Judah in Jerusalem, and he did evil in the sight of the Lord.
Then Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up, bound him with iron chains, and took him to Babylon.
Nebuchadnezzar took the Lord’s sacred vessels, brought them to Babylon, and placed them in his palace.
This was written in the book of the kings’ prophets.
Then his son Jehoiakim became king in his eighth year.
He reigned in Jerusalem for three months and ten days, and he did evil in the sight of the Lord.
In that year Nebuchadnezzar sent for him and brought him to Babylon, together with the sacred vessels of the Lord.
He made Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem when he was twenty-one years old, and he reigned for eleven years.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord and did not fear the word of the Lord spoken through the prophet Jeremiah.
King Nebuchadnezzar made him swear an oath in the name of the Lord, but he lied to him. He stiffened his neck, made his heart proud, and rejected the law of the Lord, the God of Israel.

The leaders of the people and the priests also sinned greatly and acted even more wickedly than all the nations in their impurity. They defiled [?] the Lord’s sanctuary, which had been consecrated in Jerusalem.
The Lord of their fathers sent his messenger to rebuke them and turn them back, because he had compassion on them and on their sanctuary.
But they mocked his messengers, and when the Lord spoke to them, they laughed at the prophets.
This continued until he became angry with his people, because they worshiped pride. He ordered the Persian kings of the Chaldeans to come up against them.
They came and killed their young men with the sword in the courtyard of their sanctuary. They spared neither young man nor virgin, neither old nor young; they killed them all.
They took all the Lord’s sacred vessels, large and small, as well as the Lord’s ark and the treasures of the king’s palace, and carried them to Babylon.
They burned the house of the Lord, tore down Jerusalem’s walls, and burned its fortified buildings with fire.
They destroyed all its beautiful things and took captive those who had survived the battle.
They took their men and their children to Babylon, to the king of Persia, so that the word of the Lord spoken through Jeremiah might be fulfilled.
So that the land might enjoy its Sabbaths, it rested throughout all the days of its desolation, until seventy years were completed.
In the reign of Cyrus, king of Persia, in the first year, the word of the Lord that he had spoken through Jeremiah was fulfilled.
The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus, king of Persia, and he proclaimed throughout his kingdom and put it in writing, saying:
Cyrus, king of Persia, said this: “The Lord of Israel, God Most High, has made me king over the world.
He has commissioned me to build him a house in Jerusalem in Judah.
If any of you belong to his people, may God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem in Judah and build a dwelling for the Lord of Israel, God in Jerusalem.
All of you, wherever you live in your towns, help him with gold and silver from your respective districts,
and with horses and livestock, together with everything pledged by a vow. You yourselves must also contribute to the temple of God.”

Then the leaders of the tribes in the towns of Judah and Benjamin came forward, along with the people, the priests, the Levites, and everyone whose spirit God had stirred to go up and build the house of God in Jerusalem.
Those in the surrounding regions helped them with all kinds of gold and silver, horses and livestock, with what they had pledged by vows, and with everything their hearts willingly offered.
King Cyrus brought out the sacred vessels of God that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and placed in the temple of his gods.
When Cyrus, king of Persia, brought them out, he entrusted them to Mithradates, his keeper.
From him they were handed over to Sanabassar, who had been appointed over Judah.
This was their number: one thousand gold basins, one thousand silver basins, twenty-nine silver bowls, thirty gold cups, two thousand four hundred and ten silver cups, and one thousand other vessels.
All the vessels handed over, both gold and silver, totaled 5,469.
Sanabassar took these with the captives from Babylon and brought them into Jerusalem.

Among them were those whom Artaxerxes, king of Persia, had instructed to write in their respective districts in Judah and Jerusalem: Belemus, Mithradates, Tabellius, Rathumus, Beeltethmus, Semellius the secretary, and all their subordinates who lived in Samaria and in other towns. They wrote a letter saying:
“To King Artaxerxes, their lord, from your servants Rathumus, who bows before you, Semellius the secretary, all their subordinates, and those in Coele-Syria and Phoenicia.

And now, let their lord the king know: the Jews who came up from you to us have gone to Jerusalem, that wicked and rebellious city. They are rebuilding its walls and foundations and restoring the temple.
Once that city is rebuilt and its battlements are completed, they will no longer pay tribute, and the kingdom will suffer further loss.
They are building the temple and making it beautiful. Now do not remain silent about this.
Send to King Cyrus so that they may search the books of the prophets of your ancestors.
You will find it written about this that this city rebels against kings and oppresses other cities.
The Jews too have been rebels and traitors from their beginning, and for this reason that city was destroyed.
Now, their lord the king, we inform you that if that city is rebuilt and its walls stand, they will not let you pass through Coele-Syria and Phoenicia.”

Then the king wrote to Rathumus, who had written to him, to Beeltethmus, to Semellius the secretary, and to the rest of their subordinates who lived in Samaria and Phoenicia, in reply to what they had written to him. The letter said:
“I have read the letter you sent me, and I ordered a search to be made. They found that this city has rebelled against kings from its beginning.
Its people are traitors, and murder is their practice. The kings of Jerusalem were powerful and wicked; they ruled Coele-Syria and Phoenicia and exacted tribute from them.
Now I have ordered that those people be prevented from rebuilding that city, and that no one do any work in it,
so that it does not increase the evil through what the kings do to it [?].”

After this, when Rathumus, Semellius the scribe, and those under their authority read the letter that King Artaxerxes had written, they hurried on horseback to Jerusalem with many people and began to stop those who were building.
The construction of the temple in Jerusalem was suspended until the second year of the reign of Darius, king of Persia.
King Darius held a great feast for his whole kingdom, all his people, and all the nobles of Media and Persia.
It was also for all the princes, governors, and officials throughout the hundred and twenty-seven provinces, from India to Ethiopia.
They ate and drank until they were satisfied, and afterward they went inside. King Darius entered his chamber, lay down, and slept.
There were three young men, his personal guards, who guarded the king. They said to one another:

“Come, let each of us make one statement, and let us determine what is strongest. King Darius will give many gifts to the one whose statement is wiser than his companion’s, and award him the prize for victory.
He will be clothed in purple, drink from gold, sleep on gold, ride in a golden chariot, wrap himself in purple, and wear a chain around his neck.
He will sit next to the king because of his wisdom and will become the king’s kinsman.”
Then each of them wrote his own statement, sealed it, and placed it under King Darius’s pillow.

They said, “When the king wakes up, we will give him this document. Let the king and his three Persian governors judge whom they favor, and let them award the verdict to the one whose statement is wisest, according to what they have written.”
One wrote, “Wine is strongest.”
The second wrote, “The king is strongest.”
The third wrote, saying, “Women are strongest, but truth is stronger than everything.”
Then, when the king awoke, they took the writing and gave it to him, and he read it.
He sent orders to summon all his governors of Persia and Media, as well as the princes, officials, nobles, and messengers.
They sat in his audience chamber, and the writing was read before them.
He said, “Summon these young men, and let them explain their statements themselves.” They summoned them, and they came in.
He said to them, “Present your statements.” The first, who had said, “Wine is strongest,” began to speak.
He spoke as follows: “Men, see how powerful wine is! It leads astray the mind of everyone who drinks it.
It makes the minds of the king and the mortal alike, those of the slave and the free, the poor and the rich.
It turns everyone’s mind toward joy and makes them glad, so that they do not remember any sorrow or distress.
It makes everyone feel rich. They do not remember the king or think of God, and it makes them speak grandly to everyone.
When they drink it, a friend forgets his friend and a brother his brother, and it makes them draw their swords.
When they sober up from their wine, they do not remember what they did.
Men, is not wine the strongest, since it does such things?” After saying this, he fell silent.
The second, who had said, “The king is strongest,” began to speak.
He said, “Men, do not human beings conquer the earth and rule the sea and everything in it?
Yet the king is their lord. He holds them in subjection and rules them, and they do everything he commands.”
If he tells them, “Kill your companions,” they kill them. If he sends them to war, they go and demolish mountains, [?], and fortresses.
They kill and are themselves killed, so that they do not disobey the king’s command. If they win, they bring the king [?] and everything they have plundered and captured.
Those who do not wage war or fight, but cultivate the land, also bring tribute to the king when they sow and harvest. They compel their companions to bring tribute to the king.
Yet he is just one man, all alone. If he says, “Kill,” they kill; if he says, “Spare,” they spare.
If he says, “Flog,” they flog; if he says, “Build,” they build; if he says, “Destroy,” they destroy.
If he says, “Cut down,” they cut down; if he says, “Plant,” they plant.
All the people and the whole army obey him, this one man. Yet amid all this, he reclines, eats, drinks, and sleeps.
Others keep watch around him. Not one of them can go and carry out his own wishes, nor can they refuse to obey him.
“Men, is not the king stronger, since they obey him like this?” Then he fell silent.
The third man, who had spoken about women and about truth, began to speak. He was Zerubbabel.
He said, “Men, is not the king great? Are not people numerous, and is not wine strong? Who, then, rules them and commands them? Is it not women?
They gave birth to the king and to all the people who rule the sea and the land.
From them these people were born, and they raised those who plant the vineyard from which wine comes.
They make clothes for people, and they bring honor to men. Men cannot do without women.
Even if they have gathered gold, silver, and every fine possession, and then see one beautiful woman, lovely to look at—
They forget all these things and gaze at her, looking at her face. Everyone admires her and prefers her to gold, silver, and every fine possession.
A man leaves his father, who brought him up, and leaves his country and follows his wife.
He devotes his life to his wife and does not remember his father, his mother, or his country.
From this too you know that women have power over you. Do you not bring all the fruits of your toil and labor to women and give them to them?
A man takes his spear, goes out, travels, steals, and journeys across seas and rivers.
He travels in darkness, and even when he sees a lion, he keeps going. When he has stolen, plundered, and gone on his way, he brings it to her.
A man prefers his wife to his father and mother, who brought him into the world.
Many have lost their minds because of women, have been enslaved, and have become servants because of them.
Many have died because of women; others have gone astray, and others have sinned.
Even now, if you do not believe me, is not the king great in his authority? Do not all the nations look at him and fear to touch him?
Look: Apame, the daughter of the distinguished Bartacus and the king's concubine, sits at the king's right hand.
She takes the crown from the king's head and places it on her own head, and she slaps the king with her left hand.
Yet despite all this, the king watches her face. If she laughs, he laughs; if she becomes angry, he pleads with her to speak and to calm her anger.
Men, are not women stronger, since they do such things?”
Then the king and his governors looked at one another, and he began to speak about truth.

He said, “You men, do not women prevail? The earth is great, and heaven is high, and the sun runs swiftly, circling heaven. As it runs, it returns to its right-hand side and its place in a single day.
Is not the one who does this great? Yet truth prevails and is greater than everything.
The whole world calls upon truth, and heaven blesses it. Every work trembles and shakes, and no evil is found in truth.
Wine is unjust, the king is unjust, women are unjust, and every human being is unjust. All their works are injustice, and in all this there is no truth. They will die in their injustice.
But truth prevails forever. It is life, and it stands and remains firm forever and ever.”
With truth there is no discrimination or favoritism. Instead, she acts justly and does not dwell in injustice or evil, and everyone approves of her deeds.
There is no injustice in her judgment. She is strongest, and hers are the kingdom, the greatness, and the authority over the whole world. “Blessed be the Lord, to whom the kingdom belongs,” he said.
He fell silent. Then all the people spoke to one another and said, “Truth is great and prevails over all!”
The king said to him, “Ask for whatever you wish, beyond what is written, and I will give it to you, because you have shown wisdom. You shall live with me as my close friend and be my kinsman.”
He said to the king, “Remember the promise you made when you became king, that Jerusalem should be rebuilt,
and that you would return all the vessels taken from Jerusalem, which Cyrus brought out when he intended to destroy Babylon and promised to return there.
You also promised to rebuild the temple that the Edomites burned when the Persians devastated Judah.

Now this is what I implore you to do, my lord the king, and what I ask of you. This is the great favor I seek from you, my lord: fulfill the promise you made to the King of heaven. Carry out what came from your mouth.”

Then King Darius rose, kissed him, embraced him, and wrote letters for him to all the governors, envoys, princes, and officials, directing them to send him and all those with him who were going up to Jerusalem to rebuild it.
He wrote letters to all the governors of Coele-Syria and to those in Lebanon, instructing them to bring cedar timber from Mount Lebanon to Jerusalem and to build the city with him.

He wrote concerning all the Jews going up from the kingdom into Judah, that they and all their steadfast companions should be freed from their servitude, and that neither their governors, nor their princes, nor their officials should come to their gates.
Throughout all their territories, they were to remit their [?], and they were to leave to the Jews the fields they held.
They were to give them twenty talents each year for building the temple, until the building was completed.
For offering the continual sacrifice, which they bring every day according to their customary practice under the law, seventeen [?], another ten talents each year.
All those going up from Babylon to build the city, together with their children, were to be freed from their servitude.
He wrote concerning provisions for all the priests who went up, and the garments for the service they were to perform.
He wrote concerning the Levites that they should be given their provisions until the building of the temple in Jerusalem was completed.
He wrote concerning all those who served and worked on the city that they should be given their provisions.
He sent all the vessels that Cyrus had brought out of Babylon. He also told them to do everything just as Cyrus had commanded and to send them to Jerusalem.
Then, when the young man went out, he lifted his eyes to heaven, facing toward Jerusalem, and blessed the King of heaven.
He said, “From you comes victory, and from you comes wisdom. Glory belongs to you, and I am your servant.
Blessed are you, who have given me wisdom. In you I trust, Lord of our fathers.”
He took those letters, went to Babylon, and told all his brothers.
They blessed the God of their fathers, who had given them rest and shown them mercy.
So that they could go up and rebuild Jerusalem and the temple in which his name was invoked. They spent seven days rejoicing with harps and lyres.
After this, they selected the heads of their ancestral houses who would go up, according to their respective peoples, with their wives, sons, daughters, male servants, female servants, and livestock.
Darius sent a thousand horsemen with them to bring them safely to Jerusalem, with harps, lyres, and drums.
All their brothers joined them, and they went up celebrating.
These are the names of the men who went up, according to their companies and their peoples, each according to the boundaries of their district.

The priests, descendants of Phinehas, descendants of Aaron: Josiah son of Jozadak, son of Seraiah; and Joakim son of Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, of the house of David, of the family of Perez, of the people of Judah.
Who spoke words of wisdom before Darius king of Persia in the second year of his reign, in the month of Nisan, the first month.
These are those from Judah who came up from captivity in Persia, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had deported.

He brought them into Jerusalem, and some entered Judah. He sent them all to their respective towns. They went with Zerubbabel and Josiah son of Nehemiah, son of Zeraiah, son of Rhesa, son of Henenias, son of Mordecai, son of Beelsar, son of Aspharas, son of Barolius, son of Rohum, son of Baanah—the former leaders who had previously been appointed over them.
The number of those from the people was: the descendants of Parosh, 2,172; and the descendants of Shephatiah, 372.
The descendants of Hares: 756.
The descendants of Phethali-Moab, together with the descendants of Jeshua and Zerobani: 2,802.
The descendants of Joelam: 2; the descendants of Zathon: 970; the descendants of Corobe: 750; the descendants of Bani: 648.
The descendants of Bebai: 633; the descendants of Harge: 1,322.
The descendants of Adonikam: 39; the descendants of Bose: 2,606; the descendants of Adlio: 454.
The descendants of Azrezkiyu, the descendants of Kelan, and those of Azetos: 67; the descendants of Azer: 432.
The descendants of Hananiah: 101; the descendants of Arom and the descendants of Besai: 323; the descendants of Arsipharith.
The descendants of Baiterus, 3,005; the descendants of Bethlehem, 123.
Those from Netophah, 55; those from Anathoth, 158; and those from Bethsamon who died.
The villages of Haryos: 25; those from Piras and Rog: 700.
Those of Kedias and the Amidawians: 422; those of Keramesikabes: 621.
Those from Makalon: 122; those from Bethalion: 52; the descendants of NiphAs: 156.
The descendants of Kalamolelu and Hunes: 725; the descendants of Jericho: 245.
The descendants of Anahas: 3,301.
The priests: the descendants of Jeshua, together with the descendants of Anasib: 872; the descendants of Emmeruth: 252.
The descendants of Pashhur: 1,247.
The Levites: the descendants of Jeshua, of Kodohel, and of Banu and Sudias: 74.
The sons of the singing priests, the sons of Asaph: 128.
And the gatekeepers: 400; the Ishmaelites and the sons of Teman, the sons of Dacubi: 1,000; the sons of Tabis, all of them: 129.
And the sons of the priests: the sons of Esau, the sons of Gasoph, the sons of Tabloth, the sons of Ceras, the sons of Sud, the sons of Phaleas, the sons of Labana, the sons of Abiga.
The sons of Acua, the sons of Uta, the sons of Cetab, the sons of Agaba, the sons of Subai, the sons of Anan, the sons of Cathua, the sons of Geddur.

The sons of Jairus, the sons of Daisan, the sons of Noeba, the sons of Chaseba, the sons of Gazera, the sons of Azia, the sons of Phinees, the sons of Azara, the sons of Bastai, the sons of Asana, the sons of Meani, the sons of Naphisi, the sons of Acub, the sons of Acipha, the sons of Assur, the sons of Pharacim, the sons of Basalem.
The sons of Dida, the sons of Bacus, the sons of Sarar, the sons of Thomoi, the sons of Nasith, the sons of Atipha.
The descendants of Solomon’s servants: the sons of Esphiat, the sons of Pharida, the sons of Jeeli, the sons of Lozon, the sons of Isdael, the sons of Saphi.

The sons of Agia, the sons of Phacareth-Sabai, the sons of Sarothie, the sons of Masias, the sons of Gasi, the sons of Ades, the sons of Sabas, the sons of Apherra, the sons of Barodis, the sons of Saphag, the sons of Baadan.
All those who served the priests and the descendants of Solomon's servants numbered 372.
These are those who came up from Thermellet and Thelersas, and their leaders were Charaathalan and Aalar.
They could not establish from their clans and their families that they were Israelites. The sons of Dadan, the son of Tuban, and the sons of Necodan numbered 652.

And among the priests, those whose priestly standing could not be established were the sons of Habaiah, the sons of Jacob, and the sons of Judas, who took Augia as his wife from among the daughters of Barzillai, and she was called by his name.
They searched for him in the record of his relatives, but he was not found, and they removed him from the priesthood.
Nehemiah and Attharias told them not to give them any of the holy food until they appointed a high priest who wore the garment of revelation and righteousness.
All the Israelites aged twelve and above, excluding their male and female servants, numbered 42,360.
Their male and female servants numbered 7,337, and the male and female singers numbered 245.
There were 435 camels, 7,036 horses, 245 mules, and 5,525 donkeys.
Some of the leaders of their clans, when they reached the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem, vowed to rebuild that house on its site as far as they were able.
They pledged to bring into the temple’s offering treasury, for carrying out the work, 1,000 minas of gold, 5,000 minas of silver, and 100 priestly garments.
The priests, the Levites, and some of the people settled in Jerusalem and in the countryside; the singing priests, the gatekeepers, and all Israel settled in their respective villages.
When the seventh month began, while the Israelites were in their towns, they assembled together in the courtyard beside the eastern gate.
Jeshua son of Jozadak arose with his fellow priests, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel with his brothers, and they prepared an altar for the Lord, the God of Israel.
This was so that they could offer on it the sacrifices prescribed by the law, as written in the book of Moses, the man of God.

They withdrew, and other peoples of the land gathered with them. They arranged themselves by the altar according to their clans, because they were enemies. Then all the peoples of the land oppressed them. They offered their sacrifices at the appointed times and their offerings to the Lord in the morning and evening.
They celebrated the Festival of Booths as written in the Law, and offered sacrifices every day as before.
They also made the regular offering, the Sabbath sacrifices, and those for the new moons, and observed all the festivals as holy.
From the beginning of the seventh month, all those who had made vows to the Lord began bringing sacrifices to the Lord, although the Lord's temple had not been built.
They gave the stonemasons and carpenters their provisions: gold and silver, food and drink.
They encouraged the people of Sidon and Tyre to bring them cedar trees from Lebanon by ships over the sea to Joppa, and they wrote them a letter of authorization from Cyrus, king of Persia.

Then, in the second month of the second year after their arrival at the Lord's temple in Jerusalem, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jozadak began the work, together with their brothers, the priests, the Levites, and all those who had come to Jerusalem from captivity.
They laid the foundation of the house of the Lord at the beginning of the second month, in the second year after their arrival in Judah and Jerusalem.

They appointed the Levites to oversee the work of the Lord. Jeshua, his sons and his brothers, Kadmiel his brother, the sons of Jeshua, [?], and the descendants of Judah son of Iliadun, together with his sons and brothers—all the Levites—were appointed together as overseers to carry out the work on the house of the Lord.
The priests stood in their robes with harps and horns, and the Levites, the descendants of Asaph, praised the Lord with cymbals.
They blessed him with the psalms of David, king of Israel.
They cried out as they recited and blessed the Lord, because his glory and his goodness toward all Israel endure forever.
All the people blew horns and shouted loudly, praising the Lord at the raising of the Lord’s house.
Some of the priests and Levites who had lived there before came, clan by clan, along with the elders who had seen that house when it was built, shouting and weeping loudly.
Many others rejoiced and blew horns.
Until the people heard; and they could not hear the sound of the horn because of the people's weeping, for many people were blowing horns with a loud sound that could be heard far away.
When the enemies of the people of Judah and Benjamin heard them, they came to find out what the sound of the horns meant.
They learned that those who had returned from the place of their captivity were building the house of the Lord, the God of Israel.
They went to Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the leaders of their clans and said to them, “Let us build with you.
For we too, like you, serve your God and offer sacrifices to him, ever since Asbasareth, king of Persia, resettled us here.”
Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the leaders of the clans of Israel said to them, “It is not for us and you together to build the house of the Lord our God.”
But the nations, the people of the land who were oppressing those in Judah, harassed them, gathered together, and fought against them.
They troubled them, brought the construction to a halt, and prevented them from building throughout the reign of King Cyrus. They made them stop building until the second year of the reign of Darius.

In the second year of the reign of Darius, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied concerning the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem. They prophesied to them in the name of the Lord, the God of Israel.
Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak arose and began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem. The prophets of the Lord were with them, helping them.
In those days Sisinnes, the governor of Syria and Phoenicia, together with Shethar-bozenai and their associates, came to them and said,
“Who commanded you to build this house, roof it, and carry out all this work? And who are the builders who are building it?”
God granted favor to the elders of Judah at that time, when he showed them mercy.
They did not prevent them from building while they sent to Darius and waited for a letter to reach them.
They wrote to Darius and sent the letter, saying, “Sisinnes, governor of Syria and Phoenicia, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates, the officials in Syria and Phoenicia, to King Darius:
So that you may know everything, O king, their lord: we reached the land of Judah and came to the city of Jerusalem. In the city of Jerusalem we found the elders of the Jewish captives.
They are building a great, new house of the Lord with costly carved stone, and they have arranged timber [?] in their buildings.
The work is proceeding vigorously and advancing rapidly in their hands as they carry it out. They are doing it with great honor and diligence.
Then we questioned their leaders and said to them, "Who commanded you to build this temple and carry out this work?"
We asked them for the names of their men and the leaders of their work, so that we could send word to you and write to you about them, and we questioned their elders.
They answered us and said, "We are servants of God, who created heaven and earth."
They built this house long ago, many years before. A great and powerful king of Israel built it and completed it.
But because our fathers provoked the heavenly Lord of Israel and sinned against him, he handed them over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, king of Persia.
He also demolished this temple and burned it with fire, and took the people captive, and they brought them to Babylon.
In the first year of Cyrus’s reign in the land of Babylon, Cyrus issued a written order that this house should be rebuilt.

The sacred vessels of gold and silver that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem and placed in his palace, King Cyrus brought out again from his palace in Babylon and gave to Zerubbabel and to Sheshbazzar, the envoy.
He commanded them to take those vessels and place them in the temple in Jerusalem, and to rebuild the house of God on its own site.
Then this Sheshbazzar arrived and began working on the Lord's temple in Jerusalem. From that time until [?], they have been building it and have not finished.
And now, lord king, consider the matter and open the books of the prophets from the reign of King Cyrus that are in Babylon.
If you find that King Cyrus authorized the rebuilding of the house of God in Jerusalem, then, lord king, send us word about this matter according to your wishes.

Then King Darius ordered a search in the books of the prophets in Babylon. Something was found at Ecbatana, [?], in the province of Media, in a certain place where they kept the prophetic writings. It said the following.
In the first year of King Cyrus's reign, he commanded them to build the Lord's temple in Jerusalem, where they offer sacrifices with fire in the morning.
Its height is to be sixty cubits. Build three courses of fitted stone and one binding course of new native timber. The expenses are to be paid to them from the treasury of King Cyrus.

Also, the sacred gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar removed from the house in Jerusalem and took to Babylon, are to be returned to that house in Jerusalem, to the place where they were kept before.

He commanded Sisinnes, governor of Syria and Phoenicia, and Shethar-bozenai, their companions, and those appointed as rulers of Syria and Phoenicia to leave them their site and allow Zerubbabel, the servant of God and governor of Judah, and the elders of Judah to rebuild that house of God on its own site.
I have commanded that the people of Judah who have returned from captivity should build in every respect, consult together, and work together until they complete the house of God.
Take care to provide these men, from the revenues of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, with cattle, goats, and sheep for sacrifices to God according to the law, for Zerubbabel the governor.

Likewise, provide them continually, year by year, with the expenses for the wood they burn, the salt, the wine, and the oil, according to the amount specified by the priests in Jerusalem. (Give them whatever amount they tell you is required from the revenues.) Do not dispute with them.
So that they may bring offerings to God Most High on behalf of the king and his sons, and pray for their lives.

If there are any who refuse to act according to what is written, or who tear it down, let timber be taken from their own property and let them be hanged on it. Let their possessions be seized and become the property of the royal treasury.
Because of this, may God, whose name is invoked there, destroy all the nations and all the kingdoms that raise their hands to hinder them and to do harm to that house of God in Jerusalem.
I, Darius, have commanded that they take care to carry this out.
Then Sisinnes, governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, Shethar-bozenai, and their companions began to act as King Darius had commanded.
They themselves stood with the leaders of the Jews, urging them on and giving orders.
The sanctuary was quickly built, and they made the sacred things while the prophets Haggai and Zechariah prophesied.

They completed the work by the command of God, the God of Israel, as Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, king of Persia, had made known. It was finished in the sixth year of the reign of Darius, king of Persia.
The house was completed in the week of darkness in the month of Adar, in the sixth year of Darius’s reign.
The Israelites, the priests, the Levites, and all the people who had returned from captivity carried out what the law required, as written in the book of Moses.
For the dedication of God’s temple, they offered one hundred cattle, two hundred goats, and four hundred sheep.
Twelve goats for all the sins of all Israel, according to the number of the people under Israel's leaders.

The priests and the Levites stood in their garments, each in their own groups, for the service of the Lord, the God of Israel, according to their law in the book of Moses. The gatekeepers also stood at their respective gates.
The Israelites who had returned from captivity celebrated their Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month, because the priests and Levites had all purified themselves together.
But the children of those who had returned from captivity had not purified themselves, for all the Levites had purified themselves together.
And they slaughtered the Passover sacrifice for all those who had been taken captive and also for their brothers, the priests.
And the Israelites who had been taken captive ate—all those who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to seek the Lord.
And they celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days, rejoicing before the Lord.
For the Lord had turned the heart of the king of Persia and strengthened their hands for the work of the God of Israel.
And after this, during the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra came, the son of Azariah, son of Ezariah, son of Hilkiah, son of Shallum,
son of Zadok, son of Ahitub, son of Amariah, son of Uzzi, son of Bukki, son of Abishua, son of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, the first priest.
This Ezra came from Babylon. He knew the whole Law of Moses, which the God of Israel had given, and he was a scribe.
The king gave him honor because he had found favor in his sight, and appointed him over everything.
The Israelites went up, along with the priests, the Levites, and the priests who sang psalms [?], and [?] priests.
They went up to Jerusalem in the seventh year of the reign of Artaxerxes, in the fifth month. They had left Babylon on the first day of the first month.
And they reached Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month, as the Lord had guided them.
Ezra was very learned, and nothing escaped him in the law of the Lord or in all the commandments, judgments, and ordinances given to Israel.
And King Artaxerxes sent a letter to Ezra, the priest and scribe of the law of the Lord. The letter he sent said this:
From King Artaxerxes to Ezra, priest and scribe of the law of the Lord: greetings.

Out of love for humanity, I have considered the matter and ordered that all who wish to do so among the Jewish people, including the priests and Levites who are in my kingdom, may go to Jerusalem as they desire.
And let all who wish to go to Jerusalem and see Judah and Jerusalem join you, for I and my seven friends, my advisers, have commanded this:
that they should go and act according to the law of the Lord.
They are to bring to the Lord in Jerusalem the offering that I and my friends vowed, and all the gold and silver found in the land of Babylon for the Lord who is in Jerusalem.
Together with what the people bring to the sanctuary of the Lord in Jerusalem, let them gather the gold and silver for cattle, goats, sheep, and everything they need,
with which they will offer sacrifices on the altar of the Lord in Jerusalem, according to their law.
Whatever you wish to do with that gold and silver together with your companion, do according to the will of your God.
The sacred vessels are to be for the service of the temple of your God in Jerusalem.
And if there is anything else you need for the service of your God's sanctuary, bring it from the treasury of the royal house.

And I, King Artaxerxes, have commanded that whatever Ezra, the priest and scribe of the law of the Most High Lord, sends for should be given from my treasuries in Syria and Phoenicia. Give it, and do not delay,
up to a hundred talents of silver, also a hundred kors of wheat, and a hundred measures of wine.
And let them act according to the law of the Most High Lord, so that wrath does not come upon the king's kingdom and upon his children.
And do not take any tribute from the priests, the Levites, the priests who sing, the gatekeepers, the sons of the priests, or anyone who serves the house
of the sanctuary—not anything at all—and do not enslave them.

And you, Ezra, by the wisdom of the Lord, appoint governors and judges to judge all Syria and Phoenicia, choosing them from among all those who know the law of your God. And teach those who do not know it.

Do not fail to sentence everyone who rejects the law of your God or that of the king: some to death, some to scourging, some to imprisonment, and some to confiscation of their property, each according to his sentence.
Blessed be the Lord, who put this into my heart, for me, the king, to honor his house in Jerusalem.
For he honored us too; he honored me above kings, above all my friends, and above all the officials.
Then I trusted in the grace of the Lord my God, and I took men from Israel as companions to go up with me.
Their elders, each from their own towns, according to the jurisdictions of their territories, who go up with me from Babylon during the reign of King Artaxerxes.
From the descendants of Phoros, Thrositimos; from the descendants of Ithamar, Gamael; and from the descendants of David,
Perez and Zechariah; and 150 men were registered with him.
From [?] Moab: Eliehoenai and Zerahiah, and with him 200 men.
From the descendants of Zathoe, Iacanes, Iatel, and with him 200 men; and from the descendants of Adinuben, the son of Jonathan, and with him 250 men.
From the descendants of Lamesias, the son of Gotholias, and with him 70 men.
From the descendants of Saphatias, Zechariah son of Michael, and with him 70 men.
From the descendants of Joab, Zebadiah son of Jezelus, and with him 212 men.
From the descendants of Bani, Assalimoth son of Josaphias, and with him 160 men.
From the descendants of Beer, Zechariah son of Bebai, and with him 28 men.
And from the descendants of Astath: Johanan son of Hakkatan, and with him 110 men.
From the descendants of Adonijah, all who remained. These were their names: Eliphelet, Jeuel, and Shemaiah, and with them 70 men. From the descendants of Baneu, Baastoscurus, and with him 70 men.
I brought them to the place called the River. We stayed there for three days, and I inspected them.
We found no priests or Levites among them.
I sent to Eleazar and took with me Measmen, Anatan, Shemaiah, and Joribon, son of Nathan, son of Enatan, son of Zechariah. Along with them I took some of their leaders and wise men.
I told them to go to Iddo, the keeper of the treasury.
I instructed them to tell Iddo, his brothers, and those in that region to send us priests for the house of the Lord.
Wise men from the descendants of Mahli, the Levite, the Israelite: Asebias, his sons, and their brothers, ten of them.
Also those from the descendants of Cananeu and their children, 20 men.
There were also 220 sons of priests whom David and their leaders had brought in for the work of the Levites, and all their names were registered.
We vowed to fast there with our young people before the Lord our God and to ask for mercy for our children and our livestock.
For I was ashamed to send horsemen and infantry to secure the territory and fight against our enemies.
For we told the king that the power of our Lord is with those who seek him, to guide them in everything.
Again we prayed to the Lord concerning all this, and he showed us mercy.
I set apart twelve men from the leaders of the people, the priests, together with Sherebiah and Hashabiah, and ten men from among their brothers.
I weighed out for them the gold, the silver, and the sacred vessels of the house of the Lord, which the king, his nobles, his counselors, and all Israel had given.
I handed over to them, after weighing it, six hundred and fifty talents of silver, silver vessels weighing one hundred talents, and one hundred talents of gold.
There were also twenty gold vessels and ten bronze vessels, [?], shining like gold.
I said to them, “You are consecrated to the Lord, and the vessels are sacred. The silver and gold are an offering vowed to the Lord, the God of our fathers.

Be watchful and guard them until you hand them over to the leaders of the people, the priests, the Levites, and the leaders of Israel in their settlements in Jerusalem, inside the chamber of the house of our God.”
The priests and Levites who received the gold, silver, and vessels brought them into the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem.

They set out from that region, Theras, on the twelfth day of the first month and reached Jerusalem by the mighty hand of our God, which was with us. He saved us from all our enemies, and they reached Jerusalem.
On the third day after we arrived, they weighed out the gold and silver and handed them over in the house of the Lord to Meremoth-Uri the priest, each according to its number.
With him was Eleazar son of Phinehas, and with them were the Levites Jozabad son of Jeshua and Moeth-Sabannus.
The amount of everything was recorded at the time it was weighed.
Those who had returned from captivity brought an offering to the Lord, the God of Israel: twelve bulls and ninety-six
sheep, seventy-seven lambs, and, for deliverance, twelve young sheep. They sacrificed them all to the Lord.
Then they handed over the king’s letters to the administrators of the king’s households and to the governors of Syria and Phoenicia, and they honored the sanctuary of the Lord.
Their elders came and told me what they had done. They said to me, “The people of Israel have not separated themselves, nor have their leaders, their priests, or the Levites,
from the impurity of the foreign peoples of the land—the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Edomites.”
They and their sons married their daughters, and the holy offspring were mixed with the foreign peoples of the land. Their leaders and rulers took the lead in committing this sin.
When I heard this, I tore my clothes and my priestly garments, pulled out hair from my head and beard, and sat down sorrowful and distressed.
Everyone who feared the word of the Lord, the God of Israel, gathered around me while I was distressed over this sin, and I sat there sorrowful.
Then, at the time of the evening sacrifice, I rose from my fast, with my clothes and priestly garments torn. I knelt on my knees and raised my hands to the Lord.
I said, “Lord, Lord, I am ashamed and humiliated before your face.
For our sins are many and have risen above our heads, and our ignorance has reached heaven.
From the days of our fathers until [?], we have lived in great sin.

Because of our sins and those of our fathers, the kings of the earth took us captive, together with our brothers, our kings, and our priests. They plundered us with their weapons, and we have been humiliated to this day.
But now the Lord’s mercy toward us has become still greater: he has left us a root and a name in this holy place.
He has revealed light to us in the house of our God and has given us our sustenance while we were slaves.
Even when we were enslaved, he did not abandon us, but granted us favor before the kings of Persia so that they would provide for our needs.
So that they may honor our temple and build a wall for Zion; and they have given us strength in Judah and Jerusalem.
And now, Lord, what can we say, when this has come upon us? They have rejected your commandment, which you gave through your servants the prophets.
You told them, “The land you are entering to possess is an unclean land because of the impurity of the peoples of the land, who have filled it with their uncleanness.
Do not give your daughters in marriage to their sons.
Do not make peace with them throughout your lives, so that you may prevail over them, eat the good things of the land, and pass them on to your children forever.”
Everything that has befallen us has been because of our evil deeds and the greatness of our sins. Yet you, Lord, have been patient with our sins.
You have given us a surviving root. Shall we turn back again, reject your law, and join in the impurity of the peoples of the land?
Would you not be angry with us and kill us until you left us neither root nor offspring, nor even our name?
Lord, God of Israel, you are faithful; you have left us a surviving root to this day.
And now we are before you in our sin, though because of this we are not worthy to stand before you.

While Ezra was praying and making confession, weeping on his knees before the temple, many people gathered around him, especially those from Jerusalem—men, women, and girls. Great weeping came upon them all.
Jeconiah son of Jeiel, one of the Israelites, called to him and said, “Ezra, we have sinned against God by marrying foreign women from among the other peoples of the land.
Now this rests upon all Israel. But let us swear to God that we will send away from us all the women we have married from among the other peoples of the land, together with their children.
In accordance with your judgment and that of all who desire the law of God, rise and make them swear an oath.
For this task rests upon you, and we are with you to help.”
Ezra rose and made the leaders of the people, the priests, and the Levites of all Israel swear to do this, and they swore.
Ezra rose from the temple courtyard and went to the house of Jonah son of Nasib.
He stayed there and ate no food and drank no water, mourning over their many great sins.
Then they proclaimed throughout Judah and Jerusalem to all who had returned from captivity that they should assemble in Jerusalem.

All who were not present and did not arrive within two or three days were to be condemned according to the judgment of their leaders under their law. Their livestock were to be killed, and they themselves were to be expelled from their people.
The people of Judah and Benjamin gathered in Jerusalem within three days, on the fifth day of the waning moon in the ninth month.
They all sat in the temple courtyard, shivering from the cold, for it was the rainy season.
Ezra rose and said to them, “You have sinned by marrying women from other nations, and you have added to Israel’s sin.
Now make confession to the Lord and praise him, the God of our fathers.
Do his will and separate yourselves from the peoples of the land and from other kindred.”
They all cried out together and said to him in a loud voice, “Yes, we will do as you have commanded us.
But the people are many, and it is the rainy season in the land, so we cannot do it quickly. Nor is this the work of one day or two days, for we have sinned greatly in this matter.”
And now let all the rulers come, and let everyone gather in the towns. Let all who have married women from foreign nations come, and summon them.
Each in his own town, together with their elders and their officials, so that God's wrath, which has come upon us because of this deed, may turn away from us.
Jonathan son of Azael and Ezechias son of Theocanus came and joined together in this matter. Moson son of Lemos, Levi, and Sabbatheus also joined them.
All who had returned from captivity did this.
Ezra the priest chose for himself men from among the elders in their towns, all identified by their own towns and their own names. They agreed to do this by the evening of the tenth month.
They finished dealing with the men who had married women from foreign nations on the first day of the first month.
Among the priests, men were found who had married women from foreign nations.
The sons of Jeshua son of Jozadak and his brothers: Matthelas, Eleazar, Joribus, and Joadanus.
They undertook to send away their wives and offered a sacrifice for their sin.
From the sons of Immer: Hananiah, Zabdeus, Manes, Samaeus, Jeremiel, and Azariah.
From the sons of Pashhur: Elionas, Maasias, Ishmael, Nathanael, Hakiledus, and Saltas.
From the Levites: Jozabad, Semeis, Konos, who is called [?], Patheus, Ahudas, and Johannes.
From the singing priests: Eliasbus and Bacchurus.
From the gatekeepers: Sallum and Tolbanes.
Among Israel, from the sons of Parosh: Hiermas, Eddias, Malchias, Maelus, Eleazar, Asibias, and Benaiah.
From the sons of Elah: Mattanias, Zechariah, Jezrielus, Jeabdius, Jeremoth, and Aedius.
And from the descendants of Zamoth: Eliadas, Elisimus, Othonias, Jeremoth, Sabathus, and Zardeus.
From the sons of Bebai: Johannes, Hananiah, Zabdeus, and Hemates.
From the sons of Mani: Lemos, Mamuchus, Jadeus, Jasubus, Asahelus, and Jeremoth.
From the sons of Addi: Nahathus, Mohasias, Lacunus, Nedus, Beskaspesmis, Sesthel, Balnus, and Manasias.
From the sons of Hanan: Eliolas, Asias, Malchias, Sabus, and Simon the Kosamite.
From the sons of Asom: Meltaneus, Mattathias, Baneus, Eliphleb, Manasseh, and Shimei.

And from the descendants of Bani: Jeremiah, Mon[?], Samael, Joel, Mamdai, Pedias, Anas, Carabasion, Anasibus, Mantanemus, Elias, Bannus, Eliali, Samis, Selemias, and Nathanias. And from the descendants of Ezra: Sesis, Seria, Azael, Samatis, Zambri, and Josephus.
From Nooma: Mazitias, Zabadeas, Edes, Joel, and Benaiah.
All these had married women from foreign nations, and they sent them away with their children.
The priests, the Levites, and Israel were living in Jerusalem and in their towns on the first day of the seventh month, and the Israelites returned to their own territories.
They all gathered together in the eastern courtyard near the gate of the temple.
They told Ezra the priest and scribe to bring the Law of Moses, which the Lord, the God of Israel, had given him.
Ezra the chief priest read the Law to all the people—to their men, their women, and all the priests—so that they could hear their law, on the first day of the seventh month.
He read to them beside the gate of the temple, in the courtyard, from morning until noon, before all the men and women. They all listened to the law of their Torah with all their hearts.
Ezra, the priest and scribe of the Torah, stood on a wooden platform they had made.
He placed beside him Mattathias, Sammus, Hananiah, Azariah, Uriah, Hezekiah, and Baalsamus, placing them on his right.
On his left were Phaldaius, Mishael, Melchias, Lothasubus, Nabariah, and Zechariah.
Ezra took the book before them all and sat before them, and they all honored him.
When he opened the Torah, they all rose and stood. Azariah blessed the Lord Most High, who rules over everything.
They all answered together, saying, “Amen, amen!” They raised their hands and bowed down to the ground before the Lord.
Jeshua, Annus, Sarabias, Adinus, Jacubus, Sabateas, Auteas, Maiannas, Calitas, Azariah, Jozabdus, Hananiah, and Phalias, the Levites,
taught them the law of the Lord, and they all listened together as he read to them.
The governor said to Ezra, the chief priest and scribe, and to the Levites who were teaching them all:
“This day is holy to the Lord.” They all wept when they heard the Torah.
They were told, “Go, eat a meal, and send charitable gifts to those who have nothing.
For this day is holy to the Lord. Do not grieve, for the Lord will not abandon you.”
The Levites instructed all the people, saying to them, “This day is holy; do not grieve.”
They all went away to eat, drink, and rejoice, and to give charitable gifts to those who had nothing.
They rejoiced greatly when they heard the words that had been taught to them where they had gathered.
